pro.en: South Korea convened a memorial on Friday for Korean victims of wartime forced labor at the Sado mine complex in Japan, holding the ceremony at a hotel on Sado Island in Niigata Prefecture. It was the third consecutive year that Seoul staged its own event apart from Japan's. Nine bereaved family members attended alongside Ambassador to Japan Lee Hyuk, who delivered the commemorative address.

In his address, Lee said that many Korean workers had been mobilized against their will under Japan's colonial rule. He added that remembering their pain could deepen empathy and help everyone grasp the full history of Sado as a World Heritage site. Historical records and officials indicate that more than 1,500 Koreans were put to work at the mine between 1910 and 1945, many in hazardous underground tasks, and some died in accidents. Afterwards, relatives laid flowers at the former site of a dormitory where Korean laborers had once lived.

The dispute dates to 2024, when the mines were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with South Korea's consent. Tokyo had pledged to reflect the site's whole history and to hold an annual memorial for all workers. The governments could not agree on the ceremony's name or on the wording of the remarks, so Seoul boycotted Japan's event and held its own, as it did again in 2025 with 11 family members present. Japan held its own ceremony on Sept. 12, at which an official acknowledged that Korean workers had toiled in harsh and dangerous conditions. The Korea Herald noted, however, that his remarks made no explicit reference to the forced nature of the labor.

In July 2026, UNESCO's World Heritage Committee called on Japan to clarify how the site's interpretation and presentation reflect its whole history, including the forced mobilization of Korean workers. It also asked for a follow-up implementation report by December 2027. For the moment, Seoul and Tokyo have yet to settle on a single joint ceremony despite broader efforts to strengthen bilateral cooperation. Attention now turns to Japan's report and to the arrangements for next year's commemorations.

pro.en: Fans of James Bond are awaiting word on who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007, who stepped down after 2021's No Time To Die, with BBC saying an announcement is expected in November or December and a film set to enter production in 2027 before a 2028 release.

Producer Amy Pascal said in August that year-end was a good bet and that the studio was being methodical. Final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, and some observers anticipate that Amazon MGM, which now owns the franchise, will reveal the choice on Prime Video, unlike in 2005, when Craig arrived by boat with the Royal Marines.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct and Steven Knight to write the 26th official film, whose title is unconfirmed. Knight said he intends to write the character rather than the actor. BBC lists several reported finalists, among them Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor and Callum Turner, and cautions that Craig himself was a surprise pick in 2005.

France 24 frames the search as a debate over the franchise's future, asking whether Bond should remain faithful to his traditional identity or adapt to changing attitudes. BBC says the series is about to be rebooted with a new actor and creative team, perhaps starting afresh because the ending of No Time To Die complicates a direct continuation.

Korean fans can follow the news online like audiences elsewhere, although the date and format of the announcement remain unknown, and the official name of the new Bond is the next thing to watch in November or December.

issues.title: North Korea Changes the Shape of Its Flag for the First Time Since 1948
issues.gist: North Korea has changed its flag's height-to-width ratio from 1 to 2 to 1 to 1.65. It is the first change since the country was founded in 1948, and the design stays the same.

paragraphs.en: North Korea has changed the shape of its national flag for the first time since the country was founded in 1948. The change appears in Article 166 of the revised constitution posted on Naenara, a website of Pyongyang's propaganda outlet. The flag's height-to-width ratio is now 1 to 1.65, replacing the old ratio of 1 to 2. In other words, the flag is now a little shorter in width.

pro.en: North Korea has revised the proportions of its national flag for the first time since the state's founding in 1948, according to a rewritten constitution posted online. Article 166, published on Naenara, a website run by Pyongyang's propaganda outlet, sets the height-to-width ratio at 1 to 1.65, replacing the previous 1 to 2. The Korea Herald reported that the change effectively shortens the flag's width.

The overall design remains intact, with a broad red band at the center and narrow white bands above and below it, framed by blue bands. A red five-pointed star set within a white circle likewise remains in place. The constitution says the red band represents the blood shed by anti-Japanese fighters, while the white circle and bands symbolize loyalty to the leader and the ruling party. The earlier 1-to-2 rule had remained unchanged in the law through the constitutional revision of September 2023, according to Yonhap's account of the amended text.

Observers tie the revision to Kim Jong-un's drive to cultivate his own governing style and national identity. The Korea Herald said analysts regard it as another step in a campaign built around his "two hostile states" doctrine. The paper recalled that in 2024 Pyongyang rewrote its anthem, replacing "samcholli," a traditional term for the entire Korean Peninsula, with "this world." It added that provisions on reunification were stripped from the constitution earlier this year.

Lim Eul-chul of Kyungnam University said the revision balances continuity with earlier leaders against the creation of a distinct political identity under Kim. He added that it carries further significance because it embeds the "two hostile states" doctrine in the constitution and in national symbols. Yonhap's account, citing observers, suggested that the new proportions might reflect Pyongyang's efforts to craft a fresh national image under Kim.

Because the colors and emblems are unchanged, the revision concerns proportions alone, yet it shows how a state can use even a flag's dimensions to convey a political message. For South Korean readers, it offers a modest illustration of how national symbols can carry political meaning, and attention now turns to whether other emblems will follow.

pro.en: The South Korean government pledged on Friday to exercise zero tolerance toward cheating with artificial intelligence glasses in the nationwide college entrance exam. The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as the CSAT, is scheduled for next Thursday, only days after the pledge was announced on Friday. The Office for Government Policy Coordination said such misconduct infringes upon the fair opportunities of students who have worked diligently.

The concern originated with this year's certified tax accountant examination, where the highest first-round scorer missed just one of 160 questions. That scorer earned 397.5 points out of a possible 400, a result that many test-takers regard as unrealistic and that has been linked to smart glasses. No cheating has been established, however, and the agency administering the exam said neither of its two proctors had reported any suspicious behavior.

The Korea Herald noted that candidates in each session have about one minute per question. In one subject the average score was 30.18 out of 100, and 74.21 percent of the 16,856 candidates fell below the minimum required mark. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which administers the exam, said it was reviewing the matter, according to the Korea Herald's report. The Korean Association of Certified Tax Accountants called for a thorough investigation into the matter. Yet it said exceptional scores should not by themselves be grounds for suspicion, warning that unsupported allegations could do lasting damage to a candidate's reputation.

Officials said specialized personnel would be deployed to test sites to detect AI glasses, and that anyone caught cheating would be dealt with sternly, including through criminal complaints. The office added that it would seek an investigation into the suspicions surrounding the tax accountant exam, with the aim of clearing up the doubts thoroughly. Should cheating be confirmed, the government said it would ensure that corresponding accountability is enforced in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations.

For students sitting the CSAT, the practical implication is that specialized personnel will be checking test sites for AI glasses. The episode also illustrates how emerging technology can raise fresh questions about fairness in high-stakes examinations that determine academic and professional futures. Attention now turns to the outcome of the review of the tax accountant exam and to how the CSAT proceeds on Thursday.

The score has raised doubts among test-takers, but the agency says proctors saw nothing suspicious and is reviewing the case.
The tax accountants' association wants a thorough probe but says a high score alone is not grounds for suspicion.

pro.en: A U.S. Army officer has been arrested in Britain on suspicion of attempting to spy for Russia. The New York Times, citing two American officials, identified him as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, and said he was ensnared in a sting operation; he was detained this week and has not been convicted of any offense, while FBI Director Kash Patel said the case involved allegations of espionage.

Colonel Tyner was assigned to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, roughly 100 miles west of London, the alliance's largest base in Britain and home to troops from 20 allied nations. He has served in the Army since January 2008, was deployed to Afghanistan for a year beginning in December 2013, and holds a Bronze Star Medal.

Beyond the sting itself, it remains unclear which actions prompted the arrest. Officials said the allegations concern Russia, but it has not been established whether he actually passed sensitive information to Moscow, and the Kremlin denied any involvement, with spokesman Dmitri Peskov asserting that the detention had nothing to do with Russia.

British authorities are expected to bring charges on Sunday or Monday, after which the Army intends to pursue its own charges under military law and transfer him to the United States, according to the officials. Allies that share bases and secrets will follow the case closely, and for Korean readers it underlines how alliance security rests on trust within jointly used installations.

views.view: The NYT reports the arrest and sting but says it is unclear if he really gave secrets to Russia.

pro.en: The United Nations nuclear watchdog urged Iran on Friday to restore its inspectors' access to Iranian nuclear facilities, calling it essential to the International Atomic Energy Agency's remit to monitor Tehran's nuclear programme, in a report circulated among member states.

Iran has permitted only very limited inspections since the United States and Israel struck its nuclear sites in June 2025, and the report said Tehran had told the agency that verification could not continue in the present security climate, citing what it described as explicit and public threats of further armed aggression by the American president.

The agency described the absence of information about Iran's sites and material as a matter of proliferation concern requiring rectification with the utmost urgency, and it voiced particular unease over an underground enrichment plant near Isfahan that Tehran declared in 2025 yet has kept closed to inspectors. The report did not establish that enrichment is under way there, but it noted that the agency has been unable since the bombing to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium.

A Foreign Ministry spokesperson in Tehran said Iran remains committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty while blaming the attacks for curbing cooperation, and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi encouraged Iran to consider limited technical measures that might revive routine visits, adding that the agency stands ready to resume safeguards activities at short notice.

issues.easyKo: 튀르키예에서 열리는 유엔 기후 회의에서 각국이 전기 사용을 늘리는 목표와 화석연료를 줄이는 방법을 두고 이야기하고 있어요. 그레타 툰베리는 정부들을 강하게 비판했고, 전문가들은 합의가 쉽지 않다고 봐요. 회의는 11월 20일에 끝나요.

views.view: The Guardian reports Thunberg saying the planet is being killed and campaigners criticising slow progress on a fossil fuel phaseout.
BBC reports Oxfam's Beth John saying the prime minister cannot call for clean power abroad while approving more fossil fuels at home, while Lord Stern praised his focus on climate security.
DW says expert David Victor sees the summit as a place to talk and expects real work from smaller groups of countries.

why: The summit decides how fast countries move away from coal, oil and gas.
Current policies would still heat the planet well above the 1.5C goal.
lines.agree: Speakers agree that climate change is already harming people and that more action is needed.
lines.split: Countries disagree about whether to agree a fossil fuel phaseout and how fast to go.
lines.life: Choices on electricity and fossil fuels can affect future energy prices and jobs in clean industries.
lines.next: Watch whether countries agree on the 35% electricity goal before the talks end on Nov. 20.

paragraphs.en: The UN climate summit COP31 is under way in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to 20. Turkey is the host, and Australia is leading the negotiations. The Guardian says the talks are being held while countries still fail to cut emissions fast enough. A report by Climate Action Tracker found that current policies would heat the planet by 2.7C by 2100, well above the 1.5C goal.

pro.en: The 31st UN climate conference, COP31, is under way in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to 20, with Turkey as host and Australia presiding over the negotiations. The talks come as countries continue to fall short on emissions cuts. A Climate Action Tracker report found that current policies would warm the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, well above the 1.5C that world leaders have pledged.

Greta Thunberg, the 23-year-old Swedish activist, made her first appearance at the annual UN talks in five years and declared that the planet is "not dying, it is being killed," faulting governments for failing to avert environmental breakdown. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend, conceded that the consensus on science and climate had "gone" yet pledged a new era of British leadership, naming Dame Madeleine Alessandri as a climate security envoy.

A central aim of the summit is to lift electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 20% to 35% by 2035. DW cited an International Energy Agency analysis concluding that faster electrification could trim fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion by that date. Some governments also seek a fossil fuel phaseout, but no consensus has emerged, and because COP decisions require unanimity, any single state can derail sweeping agreements.

Campaigners and analysts have voiced doubts about progress to date. Beth John of Oxfam said Burnham's attendance sent a positive signal but insisted that delivery, not declarations, is the real test, adding that Britain cannot demand clean power abroad while approving more fossil fuels at home. Critics likewise fault Australia, a leading coal and gas exporter, for declining to set a coal phaseout date, while the expert David Victor told DW that the gathering is largely "a place where people talk about stuff" and that tangible progress is likelier to come from smaller clubs of governments and companies.

Delegates are also hearing from communities already ravaged by climate disasters, including flash floods and landslides in Nepal, while the United States, having withdrawn from the Paris Agreement, is absent. For young people in Korea, the outcome could shape future energy prices and employment in clean industries. With the talks concluding on Nov. 20, attention will turn to whether countries endorse the electrification target and any fossil fuel roadmap.

pro.en: Through nine weeks of the 2026 NFL season, ESPN’s Bill Barnwell said the year has been defined by parity, with few players or teams separating from the field, and he counted six players with a legitimate argument for Most Valuable Player.

Among rookies, Barnwell leaned toward Giants linebacker Arvell Reese for defensive honors, noting that Reese has 4.5 sacks and 14 pressures despite rushing the passer only about 11 times a game. On offense he singled out Benson, an undrafted lineman who protects Patrick Mahomes for the Chiefs and has surrendered only two sacks across eight games at left tackle.

In the Coach of the Year ranking, Barnwell placed Kyle Shanahan of the 49ers first, ahead of Liam Coen of the Jaguars and Ben Johnson of the Bears. His choice for Defensive Player of the Year was Will Anderson Jr. of the Texans, who leads the league with 9.5 sacks in eight games.

The Comeback Player of the Year race features stars who returned from serious injuries, and Barnwell ranked Mahomes first, linebacker Fred Warner second and George Kittle third. He observed that Warner has forced five fumbles in eight games, a stunning total for a player who does not primarily rush the quarterback.

For readers in Korea, the midpoint offers a convenient moment to learn the league’s teams and stars, though Barnwell stresses that his rankings reflect his own views of who deserves each award now rather than forecasts of how voters will decide.

views.view: He says the year has been even, with six real MVP cases, and he gives his own picks for each award after nine weeks.

pro.en: A federal judge in Manhattan ruled on Thursday against two US subsidiaries of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, which had sought to block UEFA from gathering evidence tied to FIFA President Gianni Infantino. Judge Jeannette Vargas found that the subsidiaries lack a direct, substantial and legally protectable interest in the proceeding.

The dispute stems from a plan, unveiled in July, under which Infantino sought to sell minority stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors. ESPN reported that investors intended to pay 4.2 billion dollars for a permanent stake of more than 20 percent in a new subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise. Each of FIFA's 211 member federations was offered 20 million dollars to approve the project, which provoked a furor and was ultimately dropped.

UEFA filed its application in August as part of a broader campaign to remove Infantino, and it has said it would lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland if it uncovers evidence of financial wrongdoing. The ruling clears the way for UEFA to seek documents from JP Morgan and the investment firm Thrive Capital. FIFA's lawyers countered that the court had not addressed the merits of the request and that no documents were yet required to be produced.

Infantino, who has run FIFA for nearly 11 years, faces the gravest crisis of his tenure, yet he intends to seek reelection in March after clearing an eligibility review by a FIFA-appointed panel. Only Kohzo Tashima of Japan, who has sat on FIFA's ruling council, has declared a candidacy so far, while UEFA is expected to back another challenger and is courting the former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger.

Prospective challengers must declare by Wednesday, November 18, so attention now turns to whether Wenger or another contender enters the race. Observers will also watch which documents UEFA is ultimately able to obtain.

pro.en: Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry exited Wednesday's game against the Houston Rockets in the first quarter and never returned, having clutched his right side before leaving for an MRI examination. Houston prevailed 115-108, snapping the Warriors' eight-game winning streak, with Kevin Durant scoring 20 points.

ESPN reported that Curry suffered an oblique abdominal tear that will keep him out for at least two weeks, covering at least the next seven games, while sources said the club was bracing for an absence closer to a month. Coach Steve Kerr conceded that concern was high, and the 8-4 Warriors were already short-handed, with center Kristaps Porzingis having stepped away from the sport.

The Warriors had gone 13-26 in the 39 games Curry missed last season, but Draymond Green argued that the team's spirit was stronger now and that it was better positioned to cope without him. Against Houston, Yaxel Lendeborg supplied 25 points and 10 rebounds and Brandin Podziemski added 22 points.

The evening also featured an ugly flashpoint late in the third quarter, when Rockets guard Marcus Smart threw a punch that appeared to graze the nose of Warriors center Charles Bassey. After a video review, Smart was assessed a Flagrant 2 foul and ejected, and Bassey dismissed the act as fake toughness, saying Smart had grabbed him earlier.

Curry is now set to miss games against San Antonio, New Orleans, Dallas, Memphis, Boston, Sacramento and Portland before his next evaluation. The team will monitor his recovery and observe how its remaining players absorb the additional burden during his absence.

views.view: Curry left early and the Warriors lost, and Kerr said his concern for the injury is high.
Curry could be out for close to a month, and the Warriors already have several injured players.
Bassey says Smart's punch showed fake toughness.

pro.en: South Korea's Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jina will travel to the United States next week for a four-day visit beginning Sunday, the foreign ministry announced on Friday. The trip is intended to advance cooperation on economic security and to reinforce the bilateral relationship between Seoul and Washington.

On Monday, Kim is scheduled to hold talks with Jacob Helberg, the US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs. According to the ministry, the two officials will discuss reinforcing supply chains as well as promoting mutually beneficial trade and investment between the two nations.

On Wednesday, the vice minister is due to attend the 10th Korea-US public-private economic forum, where she will deliver a keynote address on ways to expand bilateral economic cooperation. The address will focus in particular on the shipbuilding and energy sectors, the ministry said.

Kim also intends to meet with academic figures as part of outreach aimed at bolstering American support for Korea-US relations. The ministry said this comes at a time when the composition of the US Congress is shifting in the wake of the midterm elections held in the United States.

issues.title: South Korea's Rice Output Falls for a Fifth Straight Year
issues.gist: South Korea's rice output fell 0.9 percent in 2026 to 3.5 million tons, the fifth yearly drop in a row. The area of rice paddies also hit a record low.
issues.gistKo: 2026년 한국의 쌀 생산량이 0.9% 줄어 350만 톤이 되며 5년 연속 감소했어요. 논 면적도 역대 가장 작아졌어요.
issues.easyKo: 한국 쌀 생산량이 5년 연속으로 줄었어요. 사람들이 쌀을 덜 먹고, 정부가 다른 작물로 바꾸도록 장려하면서 논 면적도 줄었어요. 하지만 땅 한 구획당 수확량은 조금 늘었어요.

paragraphs.en: South Korea's rice production fell for the fifth year in a row in 2026. pro.en: South Korea's rice output declined for a fifth consecutive year in 2026, with government figures published on Nov. 13 putting production down 0.9 percent at 3.5 million tons. The Ministry of Data and Statistics said the harvest was the fourth-lowest since the government began compiling such data in 1965.

Cultivated acreage also contracted, with the combined area of paddies falling 1.1 percent to 670,000 hectares, the smallest on record. Yield per 1,000 square meters edged up 0.2 percent to 524 kilograms, so the decrease in aggregate production reflected a shrinking footprint of rice fields rather than weaker productivity.

Reports attributed the decline to shifting dietary habits, noting that although rice remains a staple of the national diet, consumption has steadily fallen over recent decades. The drop also coincided with government efforts to manage output and to encourage farmers to move into other crops instead of growing rice.

Regionally, South Jeolla Province and Gwangju combined to produce the largest share, at 736,000 tons, according to the government findings. South Chungcheong Province followed with 681,000 tons, while North Jeolla Province produced 526,000 tons, ranking third among the regions listed.

For Korean students, the figures illustrate how changes in everyday eating habits can reshape an entire agricultural sector over time, and why the long-run trend matters for farm policy. Attention now turns to whether the area under paddies and total output continue to fall in the years ahead, extending a downward trend that has now lasted five years.

issues.title: UK Jury Finds Two Men Guilty of Spying on Journalists for Iran
issues.gist: A London court has found two men of Iranian origin guilty of helping Iranian intelligence spy on journalists in the UK. Police say the case shows more hostile Iranian activity in Britain, and Iran denies the claims.
issues.gistKo: 런던 법원이 이란 출신 남성 두 명이 이란 정보기관을 도와 영국의 기자들을 감시한 혐의로 유죄라고 판단했어요. 경찰은 영국에서 이란의 적대적 활동이 늘고 있다고 보지만, 이란은 혐의를 부인해요.

paragraphs.en: A London court has found two men of Iranian origin guilty of helping Iranian intelligence spy on journalists in the United Kingdom. The jury at Woolwich Crown Court gave its verdicts on Thursday. The two men, both in their 40s, were hired through social media and watched the targets between August 2024 and March last year. Prosecutors said the targets included two journalists from the Persian-language channel Iran International and a lawyer.

One of them was also convicted of preparing a violent attack, while the other was cleared of that charge. A third defendant, aged 57, was cleared of all charges. One defendant said he acted under pressure because his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know he was helping Iranian intelligence. Iran has repeatedly denied the allegations.

pro.en: A London jury has convicted two men of Iranian origin of assisting Tehran's intelligence services in a scheme to spy on UK-based journalists, with verdicts delivered at Woolwich Crown Court on Thursday. The defendants, both in their 40s, were recruited through social media and carried out surveillance between August 2024 and March last year. Prosecutors said their targets included two journalists from the Persian-language broadcaster Iran International as well as a lawyer who was also being watched.

The pair visited addresses connected to their targets, took photographs and video, and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. One was also convicted of preparatory conduct tied to a violent attack, whereas the other was cleared of that charge. A third defendant, aged 57, was acquitted of every count brought against him in the trial, the Guardian and DW both reported. One defendant claimed he acted under duress because his family had been threatened, while the other said he was unaware that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence. Iran has repeatedly rejected the allegations against the two men, according to DW's account of the case.

Counter-terrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in Britain, a trend that the senior officer involved expects to continue, according to DW. The chief prosecutor described it as a calculated operation to spy on critics of the Iranian government and noted that the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place. A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company said the verdicts did not make its journalists any safer so long as Tehran continued its campaign of threats. The Guardian said the case fitted a growing tactic in which hostile states hire proxies who often have little idea whom they are targeting or why.

The United Kingdom formally designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a national security threat in July, so assisting the organization can now carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison. DW reported that the head of MI5 said in October that Iran-linked operations had produced more than 50 arrests over the past year. He added that known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled over the past decade, according to the outlet's report. European governments, DW noted, remain on heightened alert for hybrid tactics from both Iran and Russia amid recent geopolitical tensions.

Sentencing is scheduled for December 17 at the Old Bailey in London, where the two convicted men are due to learn their punishment. The case touches on press freedom and national security, themes that resonate with students who follow international news from many countries. Observers will watch the sentences handed down and whether Britain takes further measures against the Revolutionary Guard in response to such cases.

pro.en: Binance, one of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, announced on Thursday that it had completed coverage of assets affected by a vast cyberattack, committing more than $6.34 billion in company funds. The breach occurred on Oct. 29 and netted roughly $6.3 billion in digital assets, which the BBC describes as probably the largest crypto hack to date.

According to the firm, the compensation was drawn from its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, along with a futures insurance fund and its corporate treasury, while the stolen tokens were reacquired through market and over-the-counter transactions. Binance pledged to replenish SAFU to approximately $1 billion as an emergency reserve, and the BBC adds that the intruders gained access through fake job interviews.

The FBI has attributed the theft to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor, a finding that Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, dismissed as a grave political provocation. Washington and private-sector partners have so far frozen more than $2.7 billion of the proceeds, and the Justice Department said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain over $1.2 billion of that sum.

The bureau separately blamed Pyongyang for a social engineering scheme dubbed FaceStealer, which it says siphoned more than $400 million in cryptocurrency from over 900 victims during 18 months. Perpetrators lured targets into bogus video calls, urged them to click a link to repair the audio and thereby planted malware, and U.S. officials contend such thefts help finance the North Korean weapons program, an accusation Pyongyang rejects.

Because many Korean students trade digital assets or search for work online, such tactics carry real relevance at home, and the FBI cautions that even vigilant, technically savvy users can be deceived by an apparently genuine call. Attention now turns to how the courts rule on who may claim the seized funds.

The BBC highlights how North Korean hackers use fake video calls and job interviews to steal crypto.
CBS reports the FBI seized more than $1.2 billion of the stolen crypto, and officials say they will keep fighting such crime.

talk.qKo: 원화 약세는 당신의 일상에 어떤 영향을 줄 수 있나요?
talk.answer: A weaker won can make imported goods and trips abroad more expensive. Oil prices also matter because they affect many costs. I would plan my spending carefully when the exchange rate changes quickly.
talk.answerKo: 원화가 약해지면 수입품과 해외여행이 더 비싸질 수 있어요. 유가도 많은 비용에 영향을 주기 때문에 중요해요. 환율이 빠르게 바뀔 때는 지출을 신중히 계획하겠어요.

paragraphs.en: The South Korean won weakened against the US dollar on Friday, November 13, as oil prices jumped. At 3:30 p.m. the won was quoted at 1,336.7 per dollar, down 6 won from the previous close. The day before, the won had risen to 1,330.7, its strongest level in 15 days.

pro.en: The South Korean won weakened against the US dollar on Friday, Nov. 13, as a jump in oil prices unsettled markets, ending the session at 1,336.7 per dollar at 3:30 p.m., 6 won lower than the previous close, after having touched its strongest level in 15 days at 1,330.7 a day earlier.

Brent crude futures climbed 3.3 percent to $95.82 a barrel after President Donald Trump said there was no need for a deal with Iran, while Iranian media reported that oil tankers had been struck by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign investors sold a net 550 billion won, or $411 million, of local shares, and the benchmark KOSPI slipped 0.98 percent to close at 5,290.53.

The previous day had looked quite different, with foreign investors buying a net 340 billion won of local shares and exporters selling dollars, lifting the won by 2.9 won even as the KOSPI dipped 0.61 percent to 5,342.73. In two sessions, the currency thus swung in opposite directions, driven chiefly by foreign capital flows and the price of oil.

Central bank data showed that import prices fell 1.8 percent in October from the previous month, reversing a 1.9 percent gain in September, as the won appreciated 1.6 percent against the dollar and Dubai crude, South Korea's benchmark, declined 2.6 percent. Raw material prices dropped 3 percent, intermediate goods slipped 1 percent, and export prices edged up 0.7 percent.

Rising import costs are a major source of inflation because they flow into the expense of production and the prices consumers pay throughout the supply chain, the Bank of Korea has noted. A softer won combined with dearer oil could lift the cost of imported goods and overseas travel for Korean households, so attention now turns to Middle East developments and to whether foreign investors resume buying Korean equities.
